hook: The philosopher who said "I think, therefore I am", and put shapes on a grid.

pages.x: René Descartes was born in 1596 in La Haye, in France, a town now named after him. Sickly as a boy, at his school he was allowed to stay in bed until late morning, a habit he kept all his life. He said he did his best thinking there.

In 1619, as a young soldier in Germany, he spent a winter day shut in a room warmed by a stove, thinking. That night he had three strange dreams, which he took as a sign that he should rebuild all knowledge on the certainty of mathematics.
He saw that any point on a flat surface can be fixed by two numbers, how far along and how far up, so shapes can be written as equations. A story says a fly on his ceiling gave him the idea.
pages.fx: Cartesian coordinates joined algebra and geometry. Every graph, map grid and computer screen uses them.

pages.x: In his Discourse on the Method of 1637 he tried to doubt everything he could: his senses, even that he had a body. But he could not doubt that he was doubting. "I think, therefore I am." From that one sure point he tried to rebuild knowledge.
He lived in the Netherlands for twenty years, moving house often so that he would be left alone. He had a daughter, Francine, with a housemaid; her death at five was the great sorrow of his life.

In 1649 Queen Christina of Sweden invited him to Stockholm to teach her philosophy, at five in the morning, in the freezing northern winter. The lifelong late riser caught pneumonia and died in February 1650.
Descartes is called the father of modern philosophy. "I think, therefore I am" is the most famous sentence in philosophy, and his coordinates are in every graph.
